title: Rapid Fungal Diagnosis: Cryptococcal Antigen, T2Candida and Fungal PCR
summary: Learn why a negative India ink does not exclude cryptococcal meningitis, how cryptococcal antigen tests compare, what T2Candida detects directly from blood and what it misses, and how ITS sequencing and Pneumocystis PCR fit into fungal diagnosis.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 60 Hits 8 (cryptococcal diagnosis), 13 (T2Candida) and 17 (fungal molecular methods) and Trap 2 (India ink negative). Checked against Boulware 2014, Skipper 2019, Kwizera 2024, Mylonakis 2018 (STAMP), Tang 2019, Wickes 2018, Fan 2013 and Filippidis 2026 (all full text via Europe PMC). Hit 8 and Trap 2 give India ink sensitivity as <50%; Boulware 2014 found 86% overall in HIV-infected adults, falling to 42% at low fungal burden, and Skipper 2019 cites 50–86% in HIV with frequent negatives in HIV-negative patients, so the lesson teaches burden- and population-dependence (register flag rv-ch60-india-ink-sensitivity-burden). Hit 13 omits that T2Candida detects only five Candida species and that pooled specificity across studies was 94% (register flag rv-ch60-t2candida-five-species). Hit 17 says Pneumocystis PCR on BAL beats stains; Fan 2013 supports high sensitivity but notes PCR also detects colonization (register flag rv-ch60-pjp-pcr-colonization). The reviewer figures 1–3 CFU/mL and 4.2 h vs >120 h time to negativity come from a primary trial that was not openly readable and are not taught; the ITS claim about non-sporulating molds is not taught. Not taught: treatment, CrAg screening programs, BDG and galactomannan (other lessons).

objectives: Explain why India ink sensitivity depends on fungal burden and why cryptococcal antigen testing is preferred.
Compare latex agglutination and lateral flow formats for cryptococcal antigen.
Describe what T2Candida detects directly from whole blood and the species it does not cover.
Interpret ITS sequencing and Pneumocystis PCR results, including the colonization caveat.

scenes.title: Three negatives and a positive
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: three specimens. (1) CSF from an adult with advanced HIV and headache: India ink shows no encapsulated yeast. (2) An ICU patient with suspected candidemia: blood cultures still negative; the physician asks for T2Candida. (3) BAL from a transplant recipient: Pneumocystis stain negative, Pneumocystis PCR positive. Question token: “Which result do you trust?”

cues.text: Three specimens. First, cerebrospinal fluid from an adult with advanced HIV and headache: the India ink shows no encapsulated yeast.

Second, an intensive care patient with suspected candidemia and negative blood cultures, where the physician asks for T2Candida. Third, a lavage from a transplant recipient: Pneumocystis stain negative, PCR positive.
Which of these results do you trust, and what does each one actually tell you?

scenes.title: Seeing the yeast vs detecting its capsule
scenes.altText: Schematic. Card 1, India ink: a negative stain; the ink darkens the background and the thick polysaccharide capsule shows as a clear halo around the yeast; results in minutes; used on CSF. Card 2, cryptococcal antigen (CrAg): detects capsular polysaccharide in CSF, serum or plasma; latex agglutination needs sample pretreatment by heating and takes about 2 hours; the lateral flow assay (LFA) uses gold-labelled monoclonal antibodies on a strip, gives a result in about 10 minutes, is stored at room temperature. Card 3: urease agar gives a rapid presumptive identification of Cryptococcus neoformans once a yeast grows.

cues.text: India ink is a negative stain. The ink darkens the background, and the thick polysaccharide capsule of Cryptococcus shows as a clear halo around the yeast. It takes minutes and is used on cerebrospinal fluid.
Cryptococcal antigen testing does not look for whole cells. It detects the capsular polysaccharide itself, in cerebrospinal fluid, serum or plasma.

Latex agglutination needs the sample heated first and takes about two hours. The lateral flow assay is a strip with gold-labelled antibodies that reads in about ten minutes and is stored at room temperature.
Once a yeast grows in culture, a positive urease test gives a rapid presumptive identification of Cryptococcus neoformans.

scenes.title: Why a negative ink means little
scenes.altText: Schematic bar comparison from Boulware 2014 (HIV-infected adults with suspected meningitis, Uganda and South Africa): India ink sensitivity 86% overall, falling to 42% when CSF culture had fewer than 1,000 CFU/mL; CSF CrAg LFA sensitivity 99.3%, specificity 99.1%; CRAG latex about 97–98% sensitive. Among India ink–negative CSF in Uganda, Cryptococcus remained the most common pathogen. Context card (Skipper 2019): India ink sensitivity in HIV studies ranged 50–86%; in HIV-negative patients fungal burden is lower and India ink is often negative.

cues.text: India ink sensitivity depends on how many yeasts are present. In a large study of adults with HIV, it caught eighty-six percent of cryptococcal meningitis overall, but only forty-two percent when the fluid held fewer than a thousand colony-forming units per millilitre.

In the same study, the lateral flow antigen test on cerebrospinal fluid was about ninety-nine percent sensitive and specific, and latex antigen testing was about ninety-seven to ninety-eight percent sensitive.
Among India ink negative samples, Cryptococcus was still the most common pathogen found. A negative ink does not rule it out.

In people without HIV the fungal burden is usually lower, and a review notes India ink is often negative. Published India ink sensitivity in HIV ranges from about fifty to eighty-six percent, so the number depends on the population.

props.label: Ink-negative CSF: Cryptococcus still most common

props.title: Population matters
lines: HIV studies 50–86% · without HIV: often negative

scenes.title: Molecular answers and their limits
scenes.altText: Three cards. T2Candida: inside the instrument, Candida cells are lysed, the ITS2 region is amplified with pan-Candida primers, and superparamagnetic nanoparticles bind species-specific amplicons, changing the magnetic resonance signal; runs on whole blood without culture in about 3–5 hours; detects 5 species (C. albicans, C. tropicalis, C. parapsilosis, C. krusei, C. glabrata) reported in 3 groups; pivotal trial cited as 91.1% sensitive and 99.4% specific; a meta-analysis of 8 studies pooled 91% sensitivity and 94% specificity. Fungal ITS sequencing: universal primers amplify the ITS region, matched to large reference databases; some species complexes need other loci. Pneumocystis PCR on BAL: pooled sensitivity 98.3%, specificity 91.0%; can also detect colonization. Hook answers card.

cues.text: T2Candida runs on whole blood, with no culture. It amplifies a Candida ribosomal region called ITS2, and magnetic nanoparticles bind the product, changing a magnetic resonance signal. Results take about three to five hours.

It detects only five species, reported in three groups. Its pivotal trial is cited as ninety-one percent sensitive and ninety-nine point four percent specific; a pooled analysis of eight studies found ninety-one and ninety-four percent.

Other molecular tools: sequencing the fungal ITS region and matching it to reference databases identifies many fungi, though some species complexes need other genes. Pneumocystis PCR on lavage fluid pooled about ninety-eight percent sensitivity, but it can also detect colonization.
Back to the hook. The ink-negative fluid needs a cryptococcal antigen test. A negative T2Candida does not cover other yeasts. And the positive Pneumocystis PCR must be read with the clinical picture.

props.title: Hook answers
lines: 2 T2 negative: other yeasts not covered
3 PCR positive, stain negative: weigh clinical picture

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Negative India ink rules out cryptococcal meningitis” (✓ sensitivity falls at low fungal burden; order cryptococcal antigen); “Negative T2Candida rules out all yeast bloodstream infection” (✓ it detects only five Candida species); “Positive Pneumocystis PCR on BAL = pneumonia” (✓ PCR can detect colonization; interpret with symptoms and imaging).

cues.text: Trap one: a negative India ink rules out cryptococcal meningitis. No. Sensitivity falls when few yeasts are present, so order the cryptococcal antigen.
Trap two: a negative T2Candida rules out any yeast in the blood. No. It detects only five Candida species, so other yeasts are not covered.
Trap three: a positive Pneumocystis PCR on lavage fluid means pneumonia. No. The PCR is so sensitive that it can detect colonization, so read it with symptoms and imaging.

props.title: ✗ “Negative India ink rules it out.”
lines: ✓ Low burden is missed: order cryptococcal antigen

props.title: ✗ “PCR positive = Pneumocystis pneumonia.”
lines: ✓ Can be colonization: add the clinical picture

scenes.title: Flashlight vs metal detector
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “India ink is a FLASHLIGHT: it only shows yeast you can see. Cryptococcal antigen is a METAL DETECTOR: it picks up capsule material even when few cells are there. T2Candida has a FIVE-NAME GUEST LIST. PCR can hear a WHISPER (colonization), not only a SHOUT (disease).” Tokens: ink = flashlight · antigen = detector · T2 = five names. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: India ink is a flashlight; it only shows yeast you can actually see. The antigen test is a metal detector for capsule material. T2Candida has a five-name guest list. And PCR can hear a whisper, not only a shout.

Where it breaks: the antigen test is not perfect and can rarely be falsely negative; T2 groups its five species into three results; and no single test replaces culture, which is still needed to grow the organism for identification and susceptibility.

props.title: Where it breaks
lines: Antigen can rarely be falsely negative
T2 reports five species in three groups
Culture still needed for isolate and susceptibility

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Ink negative → order cryptococcal antigen”, “T2Candida: five species · PCR positive can be colonization”.

cues.text: Never let a negative India ink end the search for Cryptococcus because the capsular antigen test is far more sensitive, and remember that T2Candida sees only five Candida species while a positive Pneumocystis PCR can reflect colonization.

props.label: T2Candida: five species · PCR positive can be colonization

explanation.what: Plain language: some fungal infections are hard to see or slow to grow. Labs can look for the fungus directly with a stain, detect a piece of it (a capsule sugar or its DNA), or wait for culture. Each shortcut has blind spots. Scientific terms: India ink (negative stain), polysaccharide capsule, cryptococcal antigen (CrAg), latex agglutination, lateral flow assay (LFA), urease, T2 magnetic resonance (T2MR), internal transcribed spacer (ITS), ITS2, superparamagnetic nanoparticles, bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL), colonization.
explanation.why: India ink shows the capsule only when enough yeast are in the drop examined, so sensitivity falls at low fungal burden. CrAg tests detect shed capsular polysaccharide, so they stay positive when few cells are present. T2Candida amplifies Candida ITS2 and reads nanoparticle clumping by magnetic resonance, but its probes cover only five species. PCR detects DNA even when organisms are present without disease, so very sensitive PCR can be positive in colonization.
explanation.measure: Boulware 2014 (HIV, suspected meningitis): India ink sensitivity 86% overall, 42% when CSF culture < 1,000 CFU/mL; CSF CrAg LFA sensitivity 99.3%, specificity 99.1%; CRAG latex about 97–98% sensitive. LFA result about 10 min; latex needs heat pretreatment and about 2 h (Kwizera 2024). T2Candida: about 3–5 h on whole blood; 5 species in 3 result groups; trial figures cited as 91.1% sensitivity, 99.4% specificity; pooled 91% and 94% (8 studies). Pneumocystis PCR on BAL: pooled sensitivity 98.3%, specificity 91.0%.
explanation.differs: India ink (sees cells; burden-dependent) vs CrAg (detects capsular antigen; highly sensitive); latex (heat step, ~2 h, lab-based) vs LFA (strip, ~10 min, room temperature); T2Candida (whole blood, 5 species, no isolate) vs blood culture (slow, less sensitive, yields an isolate for susceptibility testing); PCR positive with negative stain (colonization or early infection) vs both positive.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: choose the next test after a negative India ink, pick the true statement about T2Candida, or interpret a PCR-positive, stain-negative Pneumocystis result.

mnemonic.text: India ink is a FLASHLIGHT: it only shows yeast you can see. Cryptococcal antigen is a METAL DETECTOR for capsule material. T2Candida has a FIVE-NAME GUEST LIST. PCR can hear a WHISPER (colonization), not only a SHOUT (disease).
mnemonic.explanation: Links each test to what it detects and its main blind spot.
mnemonic.limitation: Antigen tests are not perfect and can rarely be falsely negative; T2Candida groups its five species into three results rather than naming each; PCR results are not literally loud or quiet without quantitative assays; and no rapid test replaces culture for an isolate and susceptibility testing.

analogyLimitations: Cards and bars are schematic; percentages come from specific study populations and are not universal.
Performance figures for India ink and CrAg come mainly from HIV-infected adults in Africa.
takeaway: Never let a negative India ink end the search for Cryptococcus because the capsular antigen test is far more sensitive, and remember that T2Candida sees only five Candida species while a positive Pneumocystis PCR can reflect colonization.

questions.stem: CSF from an adult with advanced HIV and suspected meningitis is India ink negative. What is the best next laboratory step?

options.text: Test the CSF for cryptococcal antigen by lateral flow assay
options.rationale: Correct. India ink misses many low-burden infections; the CSF antigen test was about 99% sensitive in a large HIV study.

options.text: Report that cryptococcal meningitis is excluded
options.rationale: Incorrect. India ink sensitivity fell to 42% at low fungal burden, and Cryptococcus remained the most common pathogen in ink-negative CSF.

options.text: Repeat India ink only and wait
options.rationale: Incorrect. Repeating a burden-dependent stain does not fix its low sensitivity; antigen testing is the better test.
Incorrect. T2Candida is a whole-blood test for five Candida species and does not detect Cryptococcus.

questions.stem: Which statement about the T2Candida panel is accurate?

options.text: It tests whole blood directly and detects five Candida species, reported in three groups
options.rationale: Correct. It amplifies Candida ITS2 from whole blood and covers C. albicans, C. tropicalis, C. parapsilosis, C. krusei and C. glabrata.

options.text: It needs a positive blood culture bottle first
options.rationale: Incorrect. T2Candida runs on whole blood without prior culture.

options.text: A negative result excludes all yeast bloodstream infection
options.rationale: Incorrect. Species outside the five targets, such as C. lusitaniae or Trichosporon, are not detected.

options.text: It provides an isolate for antifungal susceptibility testing
options.rationale: Incorrect. It detects DNA and gives no living isolate; culture is still needed for susceptibility testing.

questions.stem: A kidney transplant recipient has a Pneumocystis PCR–positive, stain-negative BAL. Which interpretation is most appropriate?

options.text: Possible pneumonia or colonization; interpret with symptoms, imaging and other results
options.rationale: Correct. BAL PCR is highly sensitive but can detect colonization, so the result needs clinical context.

options.text: Definite Pneumocystis pneumonia regardless of the clinical picture
options.rationale: Incorrect. PCR detects DNA from colonizing organisms too.

options.text: A false positive, because the stain is the gold standard
options.rationale: Incorrect. PCR is more sensitive than staining, so a negative stain does not make a positive PCR false.

options.text: Proof that the organism should be cultured for confirmation
options.rationale: Incorrect. Pneumocystis jirovecii is hard to culture in vitro, which is why diagnosis relies on microscopy and PCR.

claims.text: India ink is a negative stain showing the capsule; sensitivity 86% overall in an HIV cohort, 42% at < 1,000 CFU/mL, 50–86% across HIV studies, often negative without HIV; Cryptococcus remains common in ink-negative CSF.

CrAg detects capsular polysaccharide in CSF, serum and plasma; LFA ~99% sensitive and specific in CSF, ~10 min, room temperature; latex needs heat pretreatment, ~2 h, ~97–98% sensitive; urease gives presumptive C. neoformans.
T2Candida: ITS2 PCR plus nanoparticle magnetic resonance on whole blood in ~3–5 h; 5 species in 3 groups; trial figures 91.1%/99.4%; pooled 91%/94%; no isolate.

ITS sequencing with universal primers against reference databases; some complexes need other loci; panfungal PCR on tissue more sensitive than culture; Pneumocystis BAL PCR pooled 98.3%/91.0% and detects colonization.
Reviewer figures: T2Candida detection limit 1–3 CFU/mL and 4.2 h vs >120 h time to negativity.
claims.note: Not taught; the primary trial reporting them was not openly readable.

claims.text: Reviewer: panfungal ITS sequencing identifies molds and yeasts that will not sporulate.
claims.note: Not taught; no source read stated this specifically.

claims.text: Scenario invented; cards and bars schematic.
“Ink = flashlight; antigen = metal detector; T2 = five-name guest list; PCR hears a whisper.”

accuracyFlags.issue: Hit 8 and Trap 2 give India ink sensitivity as <50%; Boulware 2014 found 86% overall in HIV-infected adults (42% at low fungal burden) and Skipper 2019 cites 50–86% in HIV, with frequent negatives in HIV-negative patients. The lesson teaches burden- and population-dependence; the practical rule (a negative ink does not exclude disease) stands.

Hit 13 omits that T2Candida detects only five Candida species (reported in three groups) and that pooled specificity across eight studies was 94% (Tang 2019), versus 99.4% in the pivotal trial cited by Mylonakis 2018.
Hit 17 says Pneumocystis PCR on BAL beats stains in sensitivity; Fan 2013 supports this but notes PCR also detects colonization, so a positive PCR with a negative stain needs clinical interpretation.
